docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
SocialJev is a family of 'classification foundation models' for the social sciences, inspired by TypeSafe's Jev. The models combine the flexibility of modern language models trained on trillions of tokens of text with the speed of lightweight NLP methods. Define your task through a simple typed interface and SocialJev returns typed outputs.

The models can be used directly through Transformers, without installing SocialJev, or through the SocialJev package, which also provides optional vLLM integrations for larger workloads.

Active development — SocialJev is under active development. Interfaces may change between early releases.

docs.title: Quickstart (Transformers)
docs.text:
A checkpoint can be loaded from Huggingface and queried directly without installing the SocialJev package:

Bash
uv pip install torch transformers pydantic
Python
from transformers import AutoModel

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)
request = model.Request(
    state="The council expanded the bus network.",
    queries=[
        model.Query(
            text="Which policy area does this document concern?",
            options=["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"],
        ),
    ],
)

results = model.query(request)
print(results[0][0].choice)
print(results[0][0].probabilities)

A possible output might be:

Text Only
Transport
{'Transport': 0.98, 'Education': 0.01, 'Healthcare': 0.01}

docs.title: Sustained workloads with the SocialJev package
docs.text:
The package provides the same typed interface across inference backends. For larger sustained workloads, its optional vLLM integration is optimized for fast inference.

The standard PyPI installation uses Transformers:

Bash
uv pip install social-jev

To include the vLLM dependencies:

Bash
uv pip install "social-jev[vllm]"

Then load the model, define a query, and submit it to the model. The package provides two methods for submitting queries:

  1. .query() submits queries synchronously
  2. .aquery() submits them asynchronously

We provide more details on the differences between the methods and different execution backends on the inference page. The example below uses vLLM with the synchronous method, which you can use like so:

Python
from social_jev import Query, Request, SocialJev

model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
)
request = Request(
    state="The council expanded the bus network.",
    queries=[
        Query(
            text="Which policy area does this document concern?",
            options=["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"],
        ),
    ],
)

try:
    results = model.query(request)
    print(results[0][0].choice)
    print(results[0][0].probabilities)
finally:
    model.stop()

The returned results have the same structure as in the Transformers example above.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
This is an early release. In particular, we are in the process of:

  1. Scaling the models and training pipeline; if these models do not yet seem to perform well on your task, consider shooting us an email and bear with us: future models will be trained on more diverse datasets and queries.
  2. Adding support for various GPU-providers so you can launch inference jobs without handling the GPU rental and setup yourself
  3. Adding a simple training interface so you can fine-tune your own model
  4. Adding an evaluation interface so you can evaluate the performance of SocialJev models under various queries easily
  5. Adding an interface to optimize SocialJev queries for your task

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The public interface consists of SocialJev and the typed inputs and outputs Query, Request, and Result.

Python
from social_jev import Query, Request, Result, SocialJev

See Concepts for the request/result structure and Inference for practical execution patterns.

docs.title: SocialJev.from_pretrained()
docs.text:
Text Only
SocialJev.from_pretrained(repo, *, backend="transformers", serve=False, **kwargs) -> SocialJev

Load a checkpoint and configure its inference backend.

Argument Meaning repo Hugging Face model repository ID or local checkpoint directory. backend "transformers" (default) or "vllm". serve Launch a managed vLLM HTTP server. Requires backend="vllm"; defaults to False. **kwargs Additional keyword arguments forwarded to the selected backend, as described below.

The checkpoint determines whether the trained head is linear or MLP. The tokenizer follows the model's revision when one is supplied.

Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained("social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview")

docs.title: Additional backend arguments
docs.text:
Beyond the explicit repo, backend, and serve arguments, additional keyword arguments are passed to the selected backend's loading or engine configuration. Their meaning and supported values are defined by that backend:

  • Transformers: arguments go to the model's from_pretrained() loader. See the Transformers model-loading reference.
  • Local vLLM: arguments go to the native engine configuration. See vLLM engine arguments.
  • Managed vLLM server: keyword names are translated to native CLI options; for example, tensor_parallel_size=2 becomes --tensor-parallel-size 2. See vLLM server arguments.

Arguments must be appropriate for the selected backend. For example, seed is a vLLM engine option; it is not a SocialJev request field or a Transformers model-loading option.

SocialJev supplies the fixed integration needed to run its trained decision head through vLLM. It otherwise leaves native execution settings to the backend's defaults or the supplied arguments.

docs.title: Example: Transformers precision
docs.text:
Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    dtype="bfloat16",
)

docs.title: Example: vLLM engine settings
docs.text:
Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
    seed=0,
    max_model_len=8192,
    max_num_batched_tokens=32768,
)

The same native engine arguments can be supplied with serve=True.

docs.title: Example: batch invariance for reproducibility
docs.text:
Batch invariance is a vLLM environment setting, not a from_pretrained() keyword argument. Set it before starting the inference script:

Bash
VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 uv run python inference.py

It reaches both local vLLM and the managed server. The engine seed already defaults to 0; a fixed seed alone does not prevent numerical differences caused by batch composition or scheduling. Our method scores options rather than randomly sampling answers, so there is no request-level sampling seed to set.

vLLM's batch-invariance mode has hardware and operation restrictions and can affect performance. Exact end-to-end batch invariance of SocialJev's custom linear/MLP inference path has not yet been validated. See vLLM batch invariance, vLLM reproducibility, and the inference guide's reproducibility section.

docs.title: SocialJev.query()
docs.text:
Python
results = model.query(requests)

Submit requests synchronously and wait for their results. Available with Transformers, local vLLM, and managed-server vLLM.

Arguments

  • requests: Request | list[Request]: one document request or a collection of document requests.

Returns

list[list[Result]], ordered first by document, then by query for that document. A single Request also produces a nested list.

Python
first_query_result = results[0][0]
print(first_query_result.choice)
print(first_query_result.probabilities)

docs.title: SocialJev.aquery()
docs.text:
Python
results = await model.aquery(requests)

Submit requests asynchronously. Available with local and managed-server vLLM, including concurrent calls on the same model.

Arguments

  • requests: Request | list[Request]: one document request or a collection of document requests.

Returns

Awaiting the call yields list[list[Result]] with the same document/query ordering as .query(). Each concurrent call returns results for its own inputs.

docs.title: SocialJev.stop()
docs.text:
Python
model.stop()

Shut down the vLLM engine workers and any managed server launched by the instance. Finish outstanding submissions first.

With Transformers, this releases the engine's model reference; calling it is not required for ordinary use.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
Python
query = Query(text="Policy area?", options=["Transport", "Education"])
  • text: str: the question defining the task.
  • options: list[str]: a nonempty list of distinct candidate answers.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
Python
request = Request(state="The bus network expanded.", queries=[query])
  • state: str: the document text.
  • queries: list[Query]: a nonempty list of queries about the document.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Each query returns a Result with:

  • choice: str: the supplied candidate answer with the highest probability.
  • probabilities: dict[str, float]: probabilities normalized over the supplied options, with keys in option order.
Python
result = results[0][0]
print(result.choice)
print(result.probabilities)

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: SocialJev expresses a task as typed requests and returns typed results. These concepts are shared by the models' direct Transformers interface and the SocialJev package, including its Transformers and vLLM backends.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text: A Query describes what you want to find out about a state. It consists of a question (text) and candidate answers (options). The question and options together define the task; the model selects among the options you supply.

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
The text field contains the question the model should answer about the state:

Python
text = "Which policy area does this statement concern?"

The question defines the comparison. Asking whether a statement mentions public transport is a different task from asking whether it supports expanding it, even if the candidate answers are the same.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The options field contains the possible answers to that question:

Python
options = ["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"]

Options are answer texts, rather than fixed numerical label IDs. Each query must contain at least one option, and its options must be distinct. Their order is preserved in the returned probability mapping.

A complete query combines both fields:

Python
from social_jev import Query

policy_query = Query(
    text="Which policy area does this statement concern?",
    options=["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"],
)

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
A Request pairs a state with the queries to answer about it. The state is the text to examine—for example, a document, a paragraph, or a statement. The query supplies the question and candidate answers introduced above.

Using the policy_query already defined:

Python
from social_jev import Request

request = Request(
    state="The council will expand the bus network.",
    queries=[policy_query],
)

A request can contain multiple queries about the same state. For example, an additional query can ask whether the statement proposes expanding a public service:

Python
expansion_query = Query(
    text="Does this statement propose expanding a public service?",
    options=["Yes", "No"],
)
request = Request(
    state="The council will expand the bus network.",
    queries=[policy_query, expansion_query],
)

Each request must contain at least one query, and different requests can contain different numbers of queries.

The same query can also be reused across states:

Python
requests = [
    Request(state="The council expanded the bus network.", queries=[policy_query]),
    Request(state="The government recruited more teachers.", queries=[policy_query]),
]

When loading a model directly through Transformers, the corresponding constructors are available as model.Query and model.Request.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Each query produces a typed Result with two attributes:

  • choice: the supplied option with the highest probability.
  • probabilities: a mapping from each supplied option to its probability.
Python
results = model.query(request)
result = results[0][0]
print(result.choice)
print(result.probabilities)

A possible output for the policy-area query is:

Text Only
Transport
{'Transport': 0.95, 'Education': 0.03, 'Healthcare': 0.02}

Results are ordered first by document, then by query for that document. Both submission methods return a nested list, including when submitting only one request.

For the request containing both policy_query and expansion_query:

Python
results = model.query(request)

results[0][0]  # First document: policy-area query.
results[0][1]  # First document: public-service expansion query.

For a collection of requests, results[1][0] would select the first query about the second document. Each concurrent submission returns results for its own requests with the same ordering.

The model assigns a score to each document–query–option combination. SocialJev converts the scores into probabilities using softmax across the options for that query. A checkpoint can use a trained linear or MLP decision head; the saved checkpoint determines which one is loaded.

Probabilities sum to one within the supplied options. Adding or changing options changes the comparison. The values are not independent probabilities for each label, nor automatically calibrated estimates of real-world certainty.

docs.title: Sync and Async inference
docs.text:
The package exposes two submission methods:

  • .query() submits requests synchronously. The calling code waits until the results are returned before continuing.
  • .aquery() submits requests asynchronously. Awaiting its results allows other asynchronous work, including other submissions, to proceed.

Both methods accept one Request or a list of requests, and both return the nested results described above. Asynchronous execution does not require a particular batch size or data source; it provides the ability to overlap work.

The default Transformers backend supports .query(). Both local vLLM and the managed vLLM server support .query() and concurrent .aquery() calls.

The inference guide explains how to choose a submission pattern and configure a workload. The API reference lists the arguments and return types.

docs.title: Inference
docs.text: This page explains how to run a SocialJev workload efficiently and reproducibly: choosing a submission pattern, processing requests, and configuring model execution. The getting-started guide introduces model loading, and Concepts explains the typed inputs and outputs.

docs.title: Choose a submission pattern
docs.text:
A prepared collection that fits into host memory can be submitted in one synchronous .query() call. This lets vLLM schedule the work internally while the application waits for the results.

When inputs or results are too large to retain together, successive .query() calls can process smaller portions sequentially. Asynchronous requests can be more efficient because they allow preparation of one batch to overlap with inference on another, while multiple batches remain in progress.

These are choices about how the application proceeds. .aquery() enables concurrency; it does not automatically make every workload faster. The appropriate submission size and number of outstanding calls depend on input lengths, available memory, and the surrounding processing.

For sustained workloads, the package provides an optional vLLM integration:

Bash
uv pip install 'social-jev[vllm]'

The examples below use local vLLM. Both .query() and .aquery() also work with the managed server described under Configure execution.

docs.title: Synchronous submissions
docs.text:
.query() accepts one request or a list of requests and waits for their results. For a prepared collection, the call is simply:

Python
results = model.query(requests)

A complete small example:

Python
from social_jev import Query, Request, SocialJev


def main():
    query = Query(
        text="Which policy area does this document concern?",
        options=["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"],
    )
    requests = [
        Request(state="The council expanded the bus network.", queries=[query]),
        Request(state="The government recruited more teachers.", queries=[query]),
    ]
    model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
        "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
        backend="vllm",
    )
    try:
        results = model.query(requests)
        print(results[0][0].choice)
        print(results[1][0].choice)
    finally:
        model.stop()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The returned results retain document order, then query order for each document.

docs.title: Submission size and memory
docs.text:
With vLLM, the collection passed to .query() is not one simultaneous GPU batch. vLLM schedules the resulting token sequences internally. The requests, their prepared inputs, and the returned results still consume host memory, so submitting everything at once is appropriate only when those fit.

Smaller successive calls allow results to be consumed before submitting more input. This remains synchronous inference; it does not require .aquery().

With the default Transformers backend, each call instead pads its sequences into one model batch. Its submission size therefore directly affects device-memory requirements as well as host-memory use.

docs.title: Concurrent asynchronous submissions
docs.text:
.aquery() allows the application to continue other asynchronous work while awaiting inference. Several calls can share one loaded vLLM model, allowing preparation and result handling to overlap with execution.

The following small script illustrates overlapping calls. Each call submits one document, but either could also receive a list of requests:

Python
import asyncio

from social_jev import Query, Request, SocialJev


async def main():
    query = Query(
        text="Which policy area does this document concern?",
        options=["Transport", "Education", "Healthcare"],
    )
    first_request = Request(
        state="The council expanded the bus network.",
        queries=[query],
    )
    second_request = Request(
        state="The government recruited more teachers.",
        queries=[query],
    )
    model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
        "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
        backend="vllm",
    )
    try:
        first, second = await asyncio.gather(
            model.aquery(first_request),
            model.aquery(second_request),
        )
        print(first[0][0].choice)
        print(second[0][0].choice)
    finally:
        model.stop()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Each call returns results for its own inputs. In this example, gather() associates the first returned value with the first submission and the second with the second submission, regardless of which completes first.

docs.title: Batch size and concurrency
docs.text:
Batch size is the number of documents included in one submission. Concurrency is the number of submissions allowed to remain in progress together. For example, 16 active calls containing 128 documents each allow up to 2,048 documents in flight. These values illustrate the relationship, rather than an optimal configuration.

Neither quantity is the GPU batch size. vLLM batches the submitted sequences internally, and each document creates one sequence per query–option combination. Input length, query count, and option count therefore affect how much work a submission represents.

For an incremental workload, the application controls when inputs are loaded, how many calls remain outstanding, and when completed results are saved or released. There is no requirement to load all batches first or accumulate all results. The small two-call example above is an illustration of concurrency, not a prescribed dataset-processing architecture.

SocialJev moves its own encoding and decoding off the caller's event-loop thread. Other loading or processing performed by the application needs to be arranged so it can overlap inference too.

The repository's Wikipedia and FineWeb runs provide concrete references for larger concurrent workloads. They include benchmark instrumentation and prepare their input collections before timed inference; they are not streaming-inference examples.

docs.title: Configure execution
docs.text:
Native vLLM options pass through from_pretrained(). For example:

Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
    max_model_len=8192,
    max_num_batched_tokens=32768,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.9,
)

These values are an example configuration, not package defaults.

docs.title: Context length
docs.text: max_model_len must accommodate a complete document–query–option sequence, including the chat-template tokens. SocialJev does not automatically truncate or split oversized documents. Splitting a document into independently scored passages changes the task and belongs in the application's input preparation.

docs.title: GPU memory and scheduling
docs.text:
gpu_memory_utilization controls vLLM's memory allocation budget. It is not a strict cap on every allocation in the process.

max_num_batched_tokens controls vLLM's token budget per scheduling step. It does not limit how many documents the package accepts in a call. Unspecified performance settings, including prefix caching and chunked prefill, use vLLM's defaults.

docs.title: Multiple GPUs
docs.text:
Native options such as tensor_parallel_size can distribute model execution across GPUs:

Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
    tensor_parallel_size=2,
)

This is a vLLM model-execution setting, independent of the number of concurrent Python submissions. Multi-GPU execution through SocialJev has not yet been validated in our smoke checks.

docs.title: Local execution and a managed server
docs.text:
Local vLLM supports both synchronous and concurrent asynchronous calls. It can handle complete collections or requests prepared incrementally.

serve=True instead launches a managed vLLM server, with the same two submission methods:

Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
    serve=True,
)

A persistent server is useful when separate applications or clients share one loaded model. The package currently launches and owns its server; attaching another SocialJev client to an already-running server is not yet exposed. Dataset size and concurrency alone are not reasons to require serve=True.

After outstanding submissions finish, model.stop() shuts down the vLLM workers and any managed server. Explicit shutdown is not required for the Transformers backend.

The API reference lists the loading arguments and submission methods.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
SocialJev scores the supplied options and returns their probabilities and highest-scoring choice. It does not randomly sample an answer, so there is no request-level sampling seed to set.

Nevertheless, floating-point scores can change with batch composition and execution scheduling. A fixed random seed alone does not prevent those differences; sufficiently close scores can change the selected option.

docs.title: Engine seed and batch invariance
docs.text:
The engine seed can be supplied through native vLLM arguments and already defaults to 0:

Python
model = SocialJev.from_pretrained(
    "social-jev/social-jev-0.6B-preview",
    backend="vllm",
    seed=0,
)

vLLM provides a batch-invariance mode intended to make results independent of the requests processed alongside them. Set its environment variable before starting the inference script:

Bash
VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 uv run python inference.py

The setting reaches both local vLLM and a managed server. It has hardware and operation restrictions, remains a beta feature, and can affect performance. See vLLM's batch-invariance documentation.
